messages.subject: Random effects in Nimble
messages.subject_clean: Random effects in Nimble
messages.body_plain:
Good morning Nimble team,

I am new to Bayesian modelling and trying to learn the ropes with Nimble using the built-in R dataset "CO2". Briefly, this dataset describes CO2 uptake as a function of concentration (continuous) and treatment (chilled or non-chilled). The experiment took place in 2 locations ("Type"), with 6 plants at each location ("Plant"), and 7 observations per plant. The design is perfectly balanced (2*6*7 = 84 observtions total).

I have had success comparing frequentist and Bayesian models until I attempted to add random effects. This is the GLMM equivalent of the model I am trying to run:

co2_glm <- lmer(uptake ~ conc + Treatment + (1|Type), data = up, REML = FALSE)

So, I am trying to add a random effect for intercept for each of the 2 values of type. (I am ignoring "plant" for now)

The model builds and compiles in Nimble without error, but throws the following error when I attempt to use configureMCMC or buildMCMC:

Error in parse(text = targetNode)[[1]][3:length(expr)] :
  object of type 'symbol' is not subsettable

## Load libraries ##
library(nimble)
library(lme4) # For GLMM

### Plant CO2 Uptake Data ###

# Copy dataset
up <- CO2

# Centre continuous variable
up$conc <- up$conc - mean(up$conc) # CO2 concentration

# Convert treatment to a dummy variable (1 = chilled, 0 = nonchilled)
up$Treatment.chilled <- ifelse(up$Treatment == "chilled", 1, 0)

# Convert group identities to integer
up$Type.num <- as.integer(up$Type)
up$Plant.num <- as.integer(substr(up$Plant, 3, 3))

### Plant CO2 Uptake - CONCENTRATION AND TREATMENT, RANDOM EFFECT FOR LOCATION BUT IGNORING PLANT IDENTITY ###

## Run standard GLMM ##
co2_glm <- lmer(uptake ~ conc + Treatment + (1|Type), data = up, REML = FALSE) # Maximum likelihood because random effects are nested and balanced
summary(co2_glm)

## Set up Bayesian model ##
code <- nimbleCode({

  # N observations
  for (i in 1:N) {
      uptake[i] ~ dnorm(mean = predicted.uptake[i], sd = sigma_error)
      predicted.uptake[i] <- alpha_grand + alpha_type[Type[i]] + beta1 * conc[i] + beta2 * Treatment[i]
  }
  for (j in 1:J) {
   alpha_type[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau_type)
  }

  # Priors
  alpha_grand ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = 1000)
  tau_type ~ dgamma(shape = 0.01, rate = 0.01)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = 1000)
  beta2 ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = 1000)
  sigma_error ~ dunif(min = 0, max = 1000)

})

## Define constants, data, and initial values ##

# Constants
N <- nrow(up) # Number of observations
J <- as.integer(max(unique(up$Type.num))) # Number of type
constants <- list(N = N, J = J)

# Data
data <- list(
  uptake = up$uptake,
  conc = up$conc,
  Treatment = up$Treatment.chilled,
  Type = up$Type.num
)

inits <- list(
  alpha_grand = co2_glm@beta[1],
  beta1 = co2_glm@beta[2],
  beta2 = co2_glm@beta[3],
  sigma_error = 1,
  tau_type = 0.01,
  alpha_type = vector(mode = "numeric", length = J)
)
for (j in 1:J) {
  inits$alpha_type[j] = co2_glm@u[j]
}

## Define Nimble model ##
nimbleOptions(allowDynamicIndexing = TRUE) # Allow dynamic indexing
co2_mod <- nimbleModel(name = "co2_mod", code = code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits, check = TRUE)

## Compile model ##
co2_mod_c <- compileNimble(co2_mod)

## Build and compile MCMC ##
co2_mcmc_config <- configureMCMC(co2_mod, print = TRUE) # Print detected conjugate relationships & default RW Metropolis sampler
co2_mcmc <- buildMCMC(co2_mod)
co2_mcmc_c <- compileNimble(co2_mcmc, project = co2_mod)

---

Eventually, I hope to build a model using the complete nested random effect structure (accounting for "type" and "plant") equivalent to the following GLMM:

co2_glm <- lmer(uptake ~ conc + Treatment + (1|Type/Plant), data = up, REML = FALSE)

But first I must figure out how to work with a single level of random effects in Nimble.

Many thanks,

George

Hi George,

Yes that error was due to a bug we caught a month or two ago and fixed in the development version. It should be fixed in the CRAN version in a few days once we have the new 0.6-7 release up.

One other comment on your example - in the model code you showed, Type is fixed and is not a parameter in the model. So if you put "Type" into 'constants' rather than into 'data', NIMBLE will carry out the MCMC more efficiently because it will recognize that Type never changes and so certain quantities in the MCMC don't need to be recalculated. That said, if your real model has a prior on Type, then you'd want to initialize Type via 'inits'.

chris

Hi George,

It looks like this is a difference between how NIMBLE processes the BUGS model code and how JAGS does it. To run this in NIMBLE, you'll need to define the distribution for each alpha_type and alpha_plant element only once.

Check to make sure I've got the nested indexing correct, but it looks to me like the following should work in NIMBLE - simply add a vector that maps from plant to type and then define each alpha_type and alpha_plant random effects only once.

constants$plant_to_type <- rep(1:2, each = 6)

code <- nimbleCode({
for(j in 1:2)

    alpha_type[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau_type)

for(k in 1:12)
    alpha_plant[k] ~ dnorm(alpha_type[plant_to_type[k]], tau_plant)
# remainder of model code...
})

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nimble Devs,

First, thanks for the great package. I find NIMBLE to be very useful and flexible.

I have been working on a problem with the goal of a complete accounting for uncertainty. The data arise in a way such that a "cut" distribution is needed (i.e. in the posterior the posterior conditional for variable B depends on variable A but the posterior conditional for A does not depend on B).

I can fit this model without fully accounting for uncertainty by first fitting the model for A and using the posterior mean of A (A_bar) to sample from [B|A_bar]. If I were to code this model by hand, I would first run the MCMC for A (without B) and get L posterior draws of A. Then, the pseudocode for MCMC iteration (k) out of K when sampling B is

1. Sample A^(k) from the first stage model fit posterior independent of the current MCMC state
    - A^(k) is a random sample from {A^(1), ..., A^(L)} ( In R: A <- A_posterior[sample(1:L, 1)])

2. Update B^(k) using A^(k)
    - B ~ [B| A^(k)]

Is there a way to do this in NIMBLE by passing the posterior of A as data and then using the sample function in R? For example, the non-working MWE

## Nimble Model
library(nimble)
code <-  nimbleCode({
  mu <- mu_post[sample(sample_vec, 1)]
  for (i in 1:N) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, sigma)
  }
  sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
})

## simulated data
N<- 100
y <- rnorm(N, 2, 3)

## "first state model fit"
L <- 1000
mu_post <- rnorm(L, 2, 0.01)

dat.fit <- list(y=y, mu_post=mu_post)
constants.fit <- list(sample_vec=1:L, N=N, L=L)
dimensions.fit <- list(mu_post=L)

model_fit <- nimbleModel(code, data=dat.fit, constants=constants.fit,
                         dimensions=dimensions.fit,
                         check=TRUE)

Hi John,

Martyn's paper suggests using multiple imputation (i.e., separate chains each based on a draw from the posterior for mu). But it sounds like you're trying to do something somewhat different - at each iteration, change the value of mu.  If you reimpute mu at a given iteration, your current sigma may not be a good value for that value of mu, so it's not clear to me that it's a good idea to do what (I think) you are trying to do. Now if one knows the full conditional for [ sigma | mu, y] and can do a conjugate update, then it would be fine because each draw of sigma would be fully consistent with the value of mu that was used at that draw, but I'm not sure whether the model you showed in your post is the actual model of interest.

chris

Soledad

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ugoline,

It's not possible to use a GPU with NIMBLE at the moment. We're exploring some possibilities in this area, so we're hoping it will be feasible in the future.

In general in R there are some packages that allow you to transfer computation to the GPU -  see here under the GPU section: https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html.  Many of those probably do indeed require an NVIDIA card. You might also see the tensorflow package for R. This allows one to do computations through tensorflow, which supports computation on a GPU.

-chris
